Consistency.justification: The proposal is strongly aligned with the core idea of developing a field-based carbon inventory for e-waste dismantling in China by matching facility electricity consumption with daily dismantling volumes across five e-waste categories. The sampling, metering, batch tracking, daily allocation, emission-factor matching, and national scaling components directly support that objective. The experiments also test the stated hypothesis against monthly averaging and proportional-allocation baselines. The related-work discussion is well integrated into the design through NILM transfer validation, controlled trials, and hierarchical uncertainty propagation. Minor gaps remain: the five product categories are not identified, and the proposal sometimes shifts from daily accounting to hourly emission-factor matching without fully explaining how hourly energy by operation or category will be reconstructed.

Clarity.justification: The proposal has a logical progression from data collection and instrumentation through NILM, allocation, emissions calculation, uncertainty propagation, and scaling. Objectives, baselines, metrics, ablations, and operational quality-control thresholds are stated clearly. The definition of NILM and the fallback allocation rules improve accessibility. However, several details remain underspecified, including the exact number of sites per stratum, the identities of the five e-waste categories, the required labeled hours per machine in the main methodology, treatment of days with multiple categories or overlapping operations, and the precise national estimator. It is also unclear how ancillary electricity loads will be assigned to categories and how daily mass records support hourly emission-factor calculations.

Novelty.justification: None of the individual components is fundamentally new: supervised NILM, submeter validation, controlled energy trials, time-varying grid emission factors, hierarchical models, and Monte Carlo uncertainty propagation are established techniques. The originality lies in integrating these components into a field-based, category-specific accounting framework for Chinese e-waste dismantling, with daily throughput matching, leave-one-site-out transfer testing, explicit fallback allocation, and variance decomposition for national estimates. This is a meaningful and potentially publishable methodological combination, but the proposal does not identify a new NILM algorithm, statistical estimator, or accounting principle that would constitute a major methodological breakthrough.

Soundness.justification: The methodology includes several strong elements: revenue-grade metering, targeted submetering, controlled trials, training-site-only hyperparameter selection, leave-one-site-out evaluation, multiple baselines, ablation studies, quality-control thresholds, and explicit propagation of meter, allocation, emission-factor, and imputation uncertainty. Nevertheless, important inferential weaknesses remain. A stratified purposive sample does not by itself justify unbiased provincial or national estimates, and the hierarchical Monte Carlo cannot eliminate selection bias without an explicit sampling model, calibration weights, or post-stratification against a defensible facility frame. Only three to four intensively labeled sites may be insufficient for evaluating cross-facility NILM generalization across heterogeneous technologies. Direct submetering is described as an oracle even though only four to eight processes may be metered and shared loads may remain unobserved. Relative allocation error can also be unstable for low-energy operations. Finally, the proposal needs explicit equations for category allocation, ancillary-load treatment, estimator weighting, covariance assumptions, and validation of interval coverage.

Feasibility.justification: The work is technically implementable with existing meters, logging systems, scales, NILM models, and Monte Carlo software, and the fallback rules provide resilience when NILM fails. However, execution is operationally demanding. Instrumenting 24 geographically distributed facilities, obtaining reliable category-level mass timestamps, conducting repeated controlled trials, maintaining hardware, and negotiating access to industrial electricity data will require substantial funding and coordination. The ablation levels of 100 to 400 labeled hours per machine appear especially burdensome when intensive labeling occurs at only three to four sites. Informal or heterogeneous facilities may lack stable production records or permit controlled trials. Small stratum sizes, participant withdrawal, incomplete submeter coverage, and limited availability of spatially matched hourly grid factors create material risks. A phased pilot, explicit staffing and budget plan, and minimum viable design would improve feasibility.

Significance.justification: Reliable carbon-intensity estimates for e-waste dismantling are relevant to life-cycle assessment, recycling policy, facility benchmarking, technology selection, and China's emissions and circular-economy planning. Replacing coarse annual or monthly assumptions with field measurements and transparent uncertainty decomposition could materially improve inventory quality and reveal where data collection or operational improvements matter most. The national and provincial outputs could therefore have meaningful policy value. The impact is somewhat constrained because electricity is only one part of dismantling's full carbon footprint unless fuels, consumables, transport, refrigerant releases, and avoided downstream burdens are explicitly outside the system boundary. Moreover, representativeness limitations could reduce confidence in national policy use.

strengths: Excellent alignment with the proposed field-based daily electricity-to-throughput accounting objective.
Strong empirical design combining metering, controlled trials, NILM validation, baselines, ablations, and uncertainty decomposition.
Clear policy relevance and potential to improve the temporal and operational resolution of Chinese e-waste inventories.
weaknesses: Purposive sampling and small stratum sizes do not yet support defensible national inference without a more explicit weighting, calibration, or selection model.
The NILM labeling plan is resource-intensive and may be too limited across sites to establish robust transferability.
Hourly emission-factor matching, shared-load attribution, mixed-category operations, and the system boundary of the claimed carbon footprint require more precise specification.
